profile.reading:
Evocative is a colocation operator whose current CEO, Arman Khalili, took over in February 2017 after previously founding CentralColo and UnitedLayer and serving as CEO of Black Lotus, later acquired by Level 3 Communications. The operators own site does not state a headquarters address, founding year, or ownership structure.

Under Khalili, Evocative acquired two former 365 Data Centers facilities, in Emeryville and San Jose, California, adding about 40,000 square feet and bringing the portfolio to five locations at the time, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Las Vegas, and the two new sites. Notably, the Emeryville facility was a reacquisition, Evocative had sold it to 365 Main in 2013 before buying it back years later, an example of a facility changing operator and then returning to its original operator, worth noting for this registrys facility-level former_operator tracking.

The company has since expanded well beyond its West Coast origin. Its current site names 10 colocation data centers across the United States, spanning California, Arizona, Georgia, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Texas, and Washington, plus points of presence in 8 additional international locations including Poland and Singapore.

The registry here tracks 2 Evocative facilities across two states, New Jersey and Virginia. Virginia does not appear among the seven US states named on the operators current site, a discrepancy worth checking during this registrys facility-level research phase. This specific facility, recorded in this registry as Evocative Santa Clara SJC11 in Santa Clara County, CA, was not individually named in the operator-level research above; its operator field was blank in the source data and is corrected here to Evocative based on the facility own name, which unambiguously identifies its operator brand. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading.body:
SJC11 publishes 73,000 square feet of technical space and no IT load figure in megawatts, making power density and AI hosting capacity impossible to assess from available data.

Floor area alone does not determine AI infrastructure suitability. A facility's capacity to run GPU-scale workloads depends on power density per square foot, which varies widely across designs and tenant configurations. SJC11's 73,000 square feet of raised-floor space signals physical scale, but without a megawatt figure, no meaningful estimate of rack count or accelerator density can be derived.

The six certifications qualify the facility for regulated workloads: SOC 2 Type 2, SSAE 18, and PCI DSS attest to operational controls and compliance environments; HIPAA qualifies it for protected health information; LEED and Green Globes rate environmental design and operations. None of these categories address power capacity or suitability for compute-dense AI training workloads. Compliance and reliability are separate problems from the power constraint that binds AI scaling.

Within California's 103 mapped data center facilities, only five publish megawatt figures, totaling 170 MW. SJC11 falls outside this five-facility set, making it impossible to rank on power or to determine whether Santa Clara County's physical concentration of compute infrastructure translates to meaningful AI hosting capacity. Operators who withhold power specifications leave their facilities' relevance to high-compute workloads opaque.
